items.caption:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says the pandemic wiped out 80% of Airbnb's business in eight weeks.

He calls it a near-death business experience that gave him clarity, and it is when he decided to get back into the details and run the company a different way.

What would you change first if your business lost 80% overnight?

Source: Lenny’s Podcast, Brian Chesky’s new playbook. Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=4ef0juAMqoE

items.caption:
Brian Chesky says the CEO of a tech company should basically be its chief product officer.

Airbnb has no CPO title. If it did, he says, it would be him. He credits a Ben Horowitz post: founders get told to delegate away the thing they are best at and hardest to replace.

Should a founder CEO ever hand off product?

items.caption:
Brian Chesky told Airbnb's leaders that leaders are in the details.

He says that is different from micromanagement, which is telling people exactly what to do. His point: if you are not in the details, how do you know people are doing a good job?

Where do you draw the line between being in the details and micromanaging?

items.caption:
Brian Chesky says going very hands-on at Airbnb was a lot more work for one to two years, then it paid off.

Once they turned the corner, everyone rowed in the same direction and he didn't have to be in meetings anymore. Culture, he says, is what happens when you're not in the room.

Would you take two hard years for a team that runs without you?

Source: Lenny’s Podcast, Brian Chesky’s new playbook. Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=4ef0juAMqoE

items.caption:
Patrick Collison says he and John decided to start Stripe because it probably wouldn't be that hard.

It was 2009. After YC's Startup School in Berkeley they got sushi, and on the walk back they decided to build the payments idea they had been kicking around. He still remembers exactly where they were on the road.

Has underestimating a problem ever helped you start something?
